description: Shani Shingnapur is a village in Newasa taluka of Ahilyanagar (formerly Ahmednagar) district, built around a shrine to Shani, the deity associated with the planet Saturn. The object of worship is a tall, self-emerged black stone that stands on an open platform with no roof, since the deity is said to prefer the open sky. According to local oral tradition, shepherds found the stone and Shani later appeared in a dream asking for regular worship. The village is also known for houses and shops with door frames but no doors or locks, a custom residents attribute to the deity's protection. The temple is managed by Shri Shanaishwar Devasthan, reconstituted under a 2018 Maharashtra Act.

description: Saptashrungi Devi Temple lies near Vani and Nanduri in Kalwan taluka of Nashik district, roughly 60 km from Nashik city, on a hill of the Sahyadri range encircled by seven peaks. The goddess, worshipped as a form of Durga, is a figure about eight feet tall with eighteen arms, each holding a different weapon, carved in relief from the natural rock face. The shrine is traditionally counted as an ardha (half) Shakti Peetha, one of the 'three and a half' in Maharashtra. Pilgrims reach it by a stairway of about 510 steps, reportedly built in 1710, or by a funicular that opened in 2018. The major fairs fall during Chaitra and the Ashwin Navaratri period.

description: Jejuri, in Purandar taluka of Pune district about 50 km from the city, is the principal centre of worship of Khandoba, also known as Malhari Martand and regarded as a form of Shiva. He is the family deity of many Maharashtrian communities. The temple crowns a hill and is laid out like a small fort, with a walled courtyard and an approach stairway lined with stone lamp pillars. During festivals devotees throw turmeric over the steps and surroundings, which gives the place its nickname Sonyachi Jejuri, or Golden Jejuri. One bell in the temple is described as a trophy from the Maratha victory over the Portuguese at Vasai, attributed to Chimaji Appa. Management lies with the Shree Martand Dev Sansthan trust.

description: Akkalkot, in Solapur district, is the main centre of devotion to Swami Samarth, a nineteenth-century saint whom followers regard as an incarnation of Dattatreya. According to Wikipedia, he came to the town in 1856, stayed about twenty-two years and took samadhi in 1878. He lived in the house of his disciple Cholappa, where the Samadhi Math stands. The Vatavruksh Mandir complex is built around the banyan tree under which he is said to have sat and taught; a tradition holds that he described himself as born of a banyan. A Solapur police tourism page notes a sabha mandap, accommodation and free meals served twice daily, and says his death anniversary is observed on Chaitra Shuddha Trayodashi.

description: Alandi, on the Indrayani river in Pune district, is the burial place of Sant Dnyaneshwar, the thirteenth-century Marathi saint who composed the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, and is counted among the founders of the Varkari tradition. According to Wikipedia, he entered sanjeevan samadhi in 1296 beneath the Siddheshwar temple complex, which also contains the Ajanvriksha tree. A temple over the samadhi is dated to roughly 1580 to 1600, with later additions by Maratha nobles, the Peshwa and the Shinde family. A news report says trustees installed a 22 kg gold kalash on the samadhi temple in August 2025. Each year the saint's padukas travel from Alandi to Pandharpur in the Wari procession.

description: Ballaleshwar at Pali, in Raigad district, is one of the eight Ashtavinayak Ganesha shrines and is unusual in being named after a devotee, Ballal, rather than the deity. According to tradition, Ballal, a merchant's son, was punished by his father for worshipping Ganesha with village children; Ganesha then appeared and agreed to remain in Pali in the stone bearing the devotee's name. The broken stone is worshipped as Dhundi Vinayak. The devasthan's history page describes restoration of an older temple from about 1751 under Baburao Phadnis, a sabhamandap built between 1902 and 1908, and repairs completed in 1932. Wikipedia describes an east-facing temple between Sarasgad fort and the Amba river. The temple is open daily with an evening aarti.

description: The Varadvinayak temple stands beside a pond at Mahad village in Khalapur taluka, Raigad district, and is counted among the eight Ashtavinayak Ganesha shrines of Maharashtra. Ganesha is worshipped here as Varadvinayak in a self-manifested (swayambhu) image that faces east with its trunk curving to the left. According to tradition, the image was found submerged in the neighbouring lake in 1690, and according to Wikipedia the present temple was built or restored in 1725 by the Peshwa-era sardar Ramji Mahadev Biwalkar. Four elephant figures guard the temple's sides, and the complex also holds images of Mushika, the Navagraha and a Shivalinga. Wikipedia adds that devotees may enter the sanctum to worship the idol directly, and that large crowds gather for Magha Chaturthi.

description: Mahaganapati Temple at Ranjangaon, in Shirur taluka of Pune district about 50 km from Pune, is one of the eight Ashtavinayak shrines of Maharashtra, where Ganesha is worshipped as Mahaganapati. The idol is also called Mahotkat and, according to Wikipedia, is described as having ten trunks and twenty hands. Wikipedia gives the main construction as 9th to 10th century while also noting that it appears to be Peshwa-era work; it records that Madhavrao I had a basement room made for the idol and that Sardar Kibe of Indore later renovated the temple. The east-facing temple has a large entrance gate topped by a nagarkhana (drum house).

description: Nageshwar Jyotirlinga Temple lies on the Saurashtra coast in Devbhumi Dwarka district, about 18 km from Dwarka city according to Gujarat Tourism. It is dedicated to Shiva as Nageshwar and is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas. According to the associated legend, the demon Daruka imprisoned the devotee Supriya, whose chanting of Shiva's name brought the god to defeat him. Tourism pages describe a large hall leading to the sanctum, an underground sanctum holding the lingam, and an 80-foot seated statue of Shiva at the site. Gopi Talav Tirth is nearby, and Maha Shivaratri is the festival most often cited. The Nageshwar claim is also made for Aundha in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand, and Wikipedia says the location of Darukavana remains debated.

description: Shamlaji, in Gujarat's Aravalli district, is a Vishnu temple on the bank of the Meshwo river, in a valley ringed by wooded hills. The black image of the deity is worshipped as Gadadhar, a name linked to the unusually large mace he holds, and local tribal communities also revere him as Kaliyo Dev, the Dark Divine. According to Wikipedia, the present building mainly dates from the 15th to 16th centuries, though construction may have begun around the 11th century, and the sanctum sculpture is probably much older, perhaps 7th to 8th century. Gujarat Tourism describes a two-storey structure of white sandstone and brick, with scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata carved on its outer walls. Devotees also bathe in the river, and a large annual fair is held at Kartik Purnima.

description: The Chamunda Mataji temple stands at the top of Chotila hill, above the town of Chotila in Surendranagar district, Gujarat. Pilgrims climb a long flight of steps to reach the shrine on the summit.

description: Mehandipur Balaji temple in Dausa district, Rajasthan, is dedicated to Hanuman, worshipped here as Balaji. According to local lore, the image manifested miraculously in the hills; no founding date or builder is recorded in the sources we checked. Alongside Balaji, the sanctum is described as holding representations of Pret Raj Sarkar and Kotwal Bhairav. The temple is best known for a tradition among devotees that attending darshan and following its rituals brings relief from what they understand as spirit affliction, and from mental and physical distress. These are matters of belief rather than established fact, and the temple's practices have also been the subject of academic and psychiatric study. The Ghata Mehandipur Balaji Trust is reported to run education, health and welfare work. Pilgrims come from Rajasthan and elsewhere throughout the year.
